Chapter 1. A Family’s Quiet Life and the First Signs of Danger.
You know, there’s something truly comforting about the rhythm of family life—especially in a home where tradition runs deep.
Picture this: a small Dutch city, where a family of watchmakers lives right above their little shop. Their days ticked by, almost in sync with the steady pulse of the clocks they crafted. The house was always open—filled with laughter, the smell of fresh bread drifting from the kitchen, and that warm feeling that, here, kindness wasn’t just expected, it was the norm.
The father was gentle—a man whose sense of fairness touched everything. His faith wasn’t just something he talked about; it showed up in the way he greeted neighbors, and how he treated customers who struggled to pay. For years, it felt like the world outside hardly mattered. Their days circled around the shop, the church, and the folks who wandered in and out of their lives.
There was almost a sense of magic, like no matter what storms were brewing far away, goodness would always find its way back home. But as the 1930s rolled on, things started to shift. News began to drift in about a new leader in Germany—someone whose words thundered with anger and certainty.
At first, these stories felt distant, like thunder rumbling on the far horizon. But then, the clouds drew nearer.
One afternoon, a neighbor showed up, worry written all over her face. She spoke quietly about new rules, about people suddenly being singled out—just because of what they believed, or where they came from. The family listened, unsettled but not yet afraid. After all, they’d always believed that love was stronger than hate, and that faith could weather any storm.
But as the months wore on, the signs grew harder to ignore. Soldiers started to appear on the streets, their uniforms a constant, chilling reminder that things had changed.
The home, once a place of warmth and welcome, slowly became a shelter for whispered conversations and worried glances. Friends who’d always been part of the community began to disappear. Some left quietly in the night. Others were taken, their absence marked by empty chairs and questions that no one could answer.
The family clung to their routines, hoping that if they just held tight, goodness would win out. But it was clear—the world they’d known was slipping away.
In all this uncertainty, their faith became the anchor. Every evening, they gathered to pray, to find comfort in the familiar words and in each other. It was in those quiet, gentle moments that courage began to take root. They didn’t know what was coming. But one thing was certain—they’d face it together.
The first signs of danger had crept in—but so had the first flickers of resolve.
